bridge: You know networks and threat modelling. Work only with fictional diagrams or expressly designated training simulators.
teaching:
### Follow the physical effect

A sensor measures a condition, a controller decides what to do, and an actuator changes something physical. A forged measurement or delayed command can matter even if no file is stolen.

### Separate safety from secrecy

A safe fallback state may differ between systems. Stopping a process can prevent harm in one setting and create harm in another. Availability, timing and integrity therefore need domain-specific analysis with responsible operators.

### Identify the old and new boundaries

Industrial, telecom and other cyber-physical systems may connect older protocols with modern remote access or cloud services. Trace authentication, command validation, timing and gateways. Do not assume that a corporate-network control automatically protects a field device.

### Practise without physical risk

Use supplied traces to identify the safety-relevant state and proposed control. Do not scan or exercise a live control network as a learning experiment. A simulator supports conclusions about its model, not an assurance that a real plant or telecom system will behave the same way.

Include monitoring, recovery and operator communication in the design. A technically possible containment action still needs an appropriate operational decision.
example:
Fictional greenhouse controller
Sensor -> control logic -> water valve
Safety constraints: never flood; do not leave plants dry indefinitely.
Fault: sensor values stop updating.
Naive security action: block every command forever.
Better design question: bounded fallback watering, alarm and manual override
under an agreed physical-risk model.
explanation: The example is deliberately low-stakes and fictional. Even here, “deny everything” can violate availability requirements. A real system needs validated physical assumptions, authority and safe operating procedures rather than a generic firewall suggestion.
exercise: Draw the control loop and identify stale input, unauthorised command and loss-of-network scenarios. For each state a possible hazard, observation and proposed safe response with an explicit assumption.
solution: Paper assumptions: this fictional greenhouse has a functioning local clock, bounded valve-open durations, a water-volume limit and a reachable manual operator. Stale sensor: hazard is repeated watering or prolonged dryness; observe an age limit on readings; stop trusting stale values, raise an alarm and use only the domain-approved bounded fallback. Unauthorised command: hazard is flooding or disabled watering; log/reject commands lacking the required authority while preserving legitimate local control. Network loss: hazard is losing remote control or alarms; continue only the validated local degraded mode and signal locally, with manual intervention planned. These are conditional design proposals. Actual durations, volumes and safe states need physical-process evidence; neither permanent shutdown nor continued watering is universally safe.
challenge: Compare a proposed automatic shutdown with a bounded degraded mode for the stale-sensor case. Explain what domain evidence and approval are needed before implementing either on real equipment.
challenge_solution: Need physical process limits, hazard analysis, validated control behaviour, operational owner approval and recovery procedures. A tabletop learning result is not permission or qualification to change live infrastructure.
